Glue — grammar

measure words (the minimal set)

Template: Number + MW + Noun (yì zhāng piào, liǎng píng píjiǔ); zhè/nà + MW (zhège, nà zhāng)

counting and pointing; gè covers almost everything when in doubt

Yào yì zhāng xiǎopiào.
Mǎi le liǎng zhī bǐ.

Foreigner traps

  • The famous five cover daily life: zhāng (flat — tickets, paper, tables), bēi (cups), píng (bottles), wǎn (bowls), zhī (pens, animals) — gè rescues everything else.
  • Two people at a table is liǎng wèi (polite) — èr is for phone numbers and math, not tables.
  • zhè/nà merge with the measure word: zhè zhāng, nà bēi — never zhè ge zhāng; the pointer fuses with the counter, not the noun.

result complements (core set)

Template: V + wán/dào/hǎo/cuò/jiàn/dǒng/diào/shàng

reports the outcome, not just the action — finished, achieved, done-well, wrongly, perceived, gone-away, closed-on

Wǒ bǎ zuòyè xiě wán le.
Tā méi zhǎo dào shǒujī.

Foreigner traps

  • V + le = did it; V + wán/dào/hǎo = did it TO COMPLETION — the complement is the point, not decoration.
  • The negative goes before the verb: méi tīngdǒng, not tīngdǒng le méi as a statement.
  • jiàn (perceive) vs dào (achieve): kànjian is the chatty twin of kàndào; jiàndào is for meeting people — three flavors of 'see'.

Native notes — gè rescue, outcomes over actions, and the yǐwéi excuse

Natives gè their way through measure words

Careful Mandarin keeps zhāng, bēi, píng, wǎn, zhī for flat things, cups, bottles, bowls, pens — but casual speech drifts toward gè everywhere else, and nobody blinks. Master the famous five, gè the rest: wrong-but-understood beats frozen silence, and hyper-correct measure words at a food stall actually sound stiff.

Result complements are the real past tense

Natives report outcomes, not bare actions: chī wán le (finished eating), zhǎo dào le (found it), tīng dǒng le (understood). A bare verb + le leaves the listener waiting — 'ate... and?'. Train the reflex: every finished action asks itself whether it was completed, achieved, or perceived, and bolts on the answer.

yǐwéi is the built-in excuse template

Wǒ yǐwéi… opens every innocent-misunderstanding confession: Wǒ yǐwéi nǐ jīntiān bú shàngbān ne! The word itself asserts you turned out wrong, so it disarms before the explanation arrives. rènwéi (to hold an opinion) never apologizes — mixing them turns an excuse into a lecture.

jiāhuo vs huǒji — pick your 'guy'

jiāhuo (guy/fellow) is everyday and safely neutral-friendly across ages. huǒji as 'buddy' skews older and folksy — a young speaker using it sounds retro on purpose. Neither works on staff or strangers: the service hail is shīfu (coming day 13), and fúwùyuán in restaurants (day 14).
